Shortage of electricity in the States 
†101. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that power projects run by the States in the country 
are not generating electricity as per their installed capacity and due to this there 
is shortage of electricity and its production cost is also increasing; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any national plan for increasing the 
production by carrying out comprehensive reforms in these projects; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) 
Generation of electricity by the power plants vis-a-vis their installed capacity 
mainly depends on their age which has a correlation with the forced outages 
and performance of the plants. The power generation of State Sector power 
projects during the period April-October, 2005 was about 171,795 Million Unit 
(MU) as against a target of 177,833 MU, representing 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
364 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
a shortfall of about 6038 MU (3.4% of target). The average electrical energy and 
peak shortage in the country during the current year (April-October, 2005) was 
7.3% and 9.1% respectively. 
The cost of generation of power varies from station to station depending upon 
the capital cost, technology used, type of fuel used and size and location of the 
plant. However, with the fixed cost remaining the same, less generation has 
the effect of increasing per unit cost of generation. 
(c) and (d) The following measures have been taken by the Government of India 
for increasing the production in the power plants: 
(i) Providing loan with interest subsidy by Power Finance Corporation to 
States under Accelerated Power Generation and Supply Programme 
(APGSP) for undertaking Renovation, Modernization and Life Extension of 
generating units. 
(ii) Introduction of Partnership in Excellence in plant performance with tie-up 
of better performing power utilities with low performing power stations to 
improve their Plant Load Factor. 
(iii) Reducing period of planned maintenance and adopting better operation 
and maintenance practices.

SHRIMATI JAMANADEVI BARUPAL:

(a) whether power reforms in the country have finally began to yield

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The trend of 
increasing commercial losses of Power Utilities has been arrested after 2001-
02. The commercial losses (without subsidy) in State Electricity Boards had 
increased from Rs. 4,560 Crores during 1992-93 to Rs. 25,259 Crores during

to improve the power situation in the country; 
(i) A capacity addition of 41,110 MW has been targeted for Tenth Five Year 
Plan consisting of 22,832 MW in Central Sector, 11,157 in State Sector

nuclear being 14,393 MW, 25,417 MW and 1,300 MW respectively.

Making Indian textile industry globally competitive 
118. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have recently decided to aodpt a number of fresh 
measures to make Indian textile industry globally competitive following the 
abolition of Multi-Fibre Arrangement w.e.f. January, 2005. 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) by when the full import of these measures will be perceptible; and 
(d) whether steps have also been taken to protect the interest of labour in the 
textile industry and if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA); (a) to 
(c) The Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to 
make Indian textile industry globally competitive. Some of the important 
initiatives taken are given as under: - 
(i) 100% Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in the textile sector under the 
automatic route. 
(ii) The Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from the SSI sector. 
(iii) The Technology Upgradation F und Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernization and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(iv) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). Incentives are 
provided for better farm practices, quality seeds, improvement in market 
infrastructure and modernisation of ginning and pressing sector. 
391 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
(v) To Provide the industry with world class infrastructure facilities for 
setting up their textile units, a new scheme namely, scheme for 
Integrated Textile Parks' has been launched by merging existing two 
schemes i.e. Textile Centres Infrastructure Development Scheme 
(TCIDS) and Apparel Parks for Exports Scheme (APES). Government of 
India support under the scheme by way of grant or equity shall be limited 
to 40% of the project cost subject to a ceiling of Rs. 40 Crores. 
(vi) Apparel Park for Exports Scheme (APES)' was launched with the 
obejective of imparting a focused thru st for setting up apparel units of 
international standards at potential growth centres, and to give a fillip to 
exports. Under APES, 12 projects have been sanctioned with an estimated 
support from Government of India of Rs. 191.70 Crores. Against the 
support of Rs. 191.70 Crores, the Government has released Rs.59.46 
Crores so far. 
(vii) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, the 
Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS)' was launched. 
Under TCIDS, 18 projects have been sanctioned with an estimated support 
from Government of India of Rs. 270.80 crores. Of this, the Government 
has released Rs. 52.57crores. 
(viii) The fiscal duty strcuture has been generally rationalized to achieve growth 
and maximum value addition within the country. Except for mandatory 
excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-made staple fibres, the 
whole value addition chain has been given an option of excise exemption. 
(ix) The import of specified textiles and garment machinery items has been 
allowed at a concessional rate of customs duty to encourage investments 
and to make our textile products competitive in the global market. The cost of 
machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy measures. 
(x) For the speedy modernisation of the textile processing sector, 
Government has introduced, w.e.f. 20.4.2005, a credit linked capital subsidy 
scheme @ 10% under TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
(xi) The National Institute for Fa shion Technology (NIFT), its seven 
branches, and the Apparel Training and Design Centres (ATDCs) are running 
various courses/programmes to meet the skilled manpower 
392 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
requirements of the textile industry, especially apparel, in the field of 
design, merchandising and marketing. 
(xii) Facilities like eco-testing laborat ories have been created to enable 
exporters to get garments/textiles pre-tested so that they conform to the 
requirements of the importing countries. 
(d) To protect the interests of labour in the textile industry, a number of steps 
have been taken by the Government such as 'Mahatma Gandhi Bunkar Bima 
Yojana', 'Health Insurance Scheme for Handloom Weavers', 'Group Insurance 
Scheme', 'Group Workshed Scheme', 'Powerloom Service Centres' etc.

SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:

country and the quantum by which it will exceed the total production registered 
during the production year 2005-06; and

and potential for future growth in different textile sub-sectors. For the year 2005-
06, the textile export target has been fixed at US$15.56 billion. 
(b) and (c) According to the industry's vision (a study by CRISIL on 
behalf of Indian Cotton Mills Federati on), the Indian textiles and apparel 
industry can achieve a potential size of US$ 85 billion by 2010, from the current 
size of about US $ 36 billion, of which, the domestic market potential would 
be US $ 45 billion and export potential would be US $ 40 billion.

Bird flu 
*53.  SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: 
SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that World Health Organisation has warned of 
spready of Bird Flu in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have taken measures to check spreading of Bird 
Flu in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) World Health Organization (WHO) has issued an alert 
that Bird Flu could spread to India and other countries from the very first time 
that the current outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5NI) was first detected in the 
Republic of Korea in December, 2003. 
Subsequently, cases in poultry and birds were reported in eleven other 
countries namely: China, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, 
Malaysia, Russia, Kazakhstan and Mongolia. 130 Human cases with 67 
deaths were reported from five countries namely: Cambodia, I ndonesia, 
Thailand, Vietnam and China (As on 17.11.2005) 
No case of Bird Flu (Avian Influenza) has been reported in India either in 
humans or birds. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry of 
Avian Influenza into India and to contain the disease if it has to happen in poultry 
or humans. The measures instituted are: 
• A joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General of Health Services consisting members from Indian Council 
of Medical Research, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 
World Health Organization and Department of Animal Husbandry is 
monitoring the situation ever si nce the WHO alerted the global 
community and advising appropriate actions to the Government. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
• The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of 
suspicion of outbreak of the disease and also in the event of 
outbreak of highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A 
conference of the State Secretarie s of Animal Husbandry was held 
regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease 
• Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal 
Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal, were found negative. 
Training has been imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the 
Animal Husbandry Department, how  to collect and dispatch the 
samples to the laboratory for testing 
• There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak 
Even birds (grand parent stock of poultry etc,) imported from highly 
pathogenic avian influenza free countries, are subjected to 
quarantine and screening. 
• Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to 
all their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory 
birds in identified water bodies Any unusual death among migratory 
birds would immediately be brought to the notice of Department of 
Animal Husbandry. 
• Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held on 1st August, 2005, with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan. 
• A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza 
has been finalized detailing immediately action to be taken to deal 
with any suspected outbreak. The state level action plan will be 
discussed with the State Governments shortly 
• The components of the action plan such as hospital strengthening, 
Influenza Surveillance Network, Laboratory strengthening in terms 
of bio-safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of 
16 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
drugs and Information Education Communication are being taken up in a 
phased manner. 
• An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under 
Chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for management of Avian Influenza in the 
country. 
• National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating 
outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human Influenza 
surveillance network has been operationalized. 
• The situation has also been reviewed by Committee of Secretaries (on a 
monthly basis) and Ministry of Home Affairs.

(c) if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARD PAWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) ICAR has been already involved in the development of location specific 
Integrated Pest Management (1PM) techniques in rice. The method advocated to 
rice farmers involves: (i) application of organic manure, (ii) early sowing and 
timely planting, (iii) use of reco mmended nitrogen fertilizer, (iv) timely 
pruning of field bunds and (v) delayed pesticide application in the crop to 
encourage build-up of natural enemies and encourage natural suppression of the 
early season pests. This method is recommended Integrated Pest Management that 
the ICAR scientists have developed over a period of research on the rice varieties 
that are released from time to time. Integrated Pest Management in rice aims at 
reduction in use of pesticides. On-farm validation of the IPM practices and 
Frontline Demostrations are also carried out to transfer the cost effective rice 
production technology to the farmers. On-farm validation of IPM Technology is 
undertaken under All India Co-ordination Rice Improvement Programme of 
Directorate of Rice Research, Hyderabad.

Seeds Bill, 2004 was introduced in Rajya Sabha in December, 2004. The Bill

Subsidy to agriculture sector 
310. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether developed countries provide adequate subsidy to agriculture sector 
in their countries compared to India and other developing countries; 
(b) whether any proposal has been mooted to provide comparable subsidy to 
agriculture sector with a view to making it globally competitive; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) Most of 
the developed countries provide very high levels of support (both domestic and on 
exports) to their agriculture sector which distort trade in agricultural commodities 
and to a large extent make agricultural products from developing countries 
uncompetitive in the international market. For instance, as per the latest 
notifications submitted by the USA and the EC to the World Trade 
Organization (WTO), the amount of domestic support provided by them was 
around US$ 72 billion and US$ 76 billion respectively as compared to support 
level of around US$ 9 billion by India and around US$ 3 billion by Brazil. 
(b) to (d) No such proposal has been mooted. However, to make the 
agriculture globally competitive in the developing countries, including India, the 
following steps have been taken for the purpose of WTO negotiations: 
(i) India alongwith like-minded/developing countires has sought 
elimination of all forms of export subsidies by a credible end-date, and 
substantial reduction in all forms of trade distorting support provided 
by the developed countries to thei r agriculture sector. In order to 
harmonize the levels of trade-distorting domestic support permitted to be 
extended to their agriculture sector by various Members, substantial 
reductions in such domestic support will be achieved through a tiered 
formula under which Members with higher levels of domestic support 
will reduce their support by a larger amount than those with a lower 
level of support. 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
(ii) The G-20, of which India is a Member, has also demanded that 
developing countries that allocate almost all de minimis support to 
subsistence and resource poor farmers should not be required to reduce the same 
as agreed to by Members in the Framework Agreement of July, 2004.

Subsidy to sugar mills 
330. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Central Government have decided to give Rs. 525 
crores subsidy to ailing sugar mills in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the number of ailing sugar mills which will be benefited by this 
subsidy; 
(d) to what extent it will help to improve our GDP; and 
(e) the details thereof, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) to (e) In pursuance to the Finance Minister's Budget Speech for 
2005-06 wherein it was announced that the sugar factories that have been 
operational in 2002-2003 sugar season will be assisted to restructure, a Committee 
was set up in NABARD to prepare a package of assistance for the sugar 
industry. Consequently, Government of India has decided that all Cooperative 
Sugar Mills in the country which have term loans outstanding as on 31.3.2005, 
and which are commercially viable and have adequate operational surplus to 
repay the said term loans will be categorized as falling under two Categories, i.e. 
Category A and Category B. Accordingly, the term loans will be 
restructured/rescheduled to enable repayment within five years (for Category A) or 
within 15 years (for Category B). The rate of interest on the restructured loans will 
be reduced to 10% per annum, with effect from 1st April, 2005, irrespective of 
the original contractual rate. Government of India will provide interest 
subvention on the restructured loan, which is estimated at Rs. 525 crores. All 
the Cooperative Sugar Mills in the country, irrespective of the State in which 
they are located can avail of the above financial assistance as per the terms and 
conditions of the package. The package will financially strengthen the Cooperative 
Sugar Mills which is turn will improve their capacity

ethanol etc. wherever applicable, which will duly contribute towards the GDP of

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) As per information received from various 
States/Union Territories (UTs) as on 31.03.2004, about 13.43 lakh hectare of forest 
land in the country is under encroachments. The State-wise details are given in the 
enclosed Statement (See below) Encroachment on forest land is an offence under Section 26 
of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and, therefore, it is required to be evicted. However; in 
September 1990, Central Government issued guidelines under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 
which enabled Central Government and the State/UT Governments to regularize pre-1980 
eligible encroachments as a one time dispensation with the condition that all post-1980 
encroaches will be evicted. However, on Supreme Court's order, Central Government on 3rd 
May 2002, directed all the State/UT Governments to evict the ineligible encroachers 
from forest lands in a time bound manner. As per reports received from various States/UTs, 
encroachments have been cleared from about 1.52 lakh hectare of forest land.

Measures taken for Tiger Conservation by Government of India 
1. Ongoing Funding Schemes: 
Funding and technical help are provided to States under the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes of "Project Tiger", "Assistance to National Parks 
& Sanctuaries" and "Project Elephant" for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastrcture of States to provide effective protection-to wild animals 
including tiger. 
2. Legal Measures Taken: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which has been amended and made 
more stringent. 
(ii) The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and 
prosecute wildlife offenders. 
3. Administrative and other Measures: 
(i) A National Wildlife Action Plan (2002-16) has been adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister 
in January 2002, which outlines the strategy for conservation and 
protection of wildlife in the country. 
(ii) Government of India has set-up regional and subregional offices for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country 
to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
4. International Conventions: 
India is signatory to many international conventions relating to 
biodiversity conservation and control of illegal trade in wild flora and 
fauna. 
5. Bilateral Agreements: 
India has bilateral agreements with Nepal and China for controlling trans-
boundary illegal trade in wildlife. 
90 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Global tiger Forum: 
A Global tiger Forum of tiger range countries has been created for 
addressing international issues relating to tiger conservation. 
7. Initiatives Taken for eliciting public support: 
Complementary inputs for Ecodevelopment and voluntary village 
relocation provided earlier in separate projects have now been merged 
with Project Tiger as an "Umbrella Scheme". 
Under the externally aided "India Eco-development Project", as many 
as 572 eco-development committees  have been formed in seven 
Projected Areas (which included six Tiger Reserves) covering 75,600 
families, to reduce the dependency of local people on Protected Area 
resources, with reciprocal commitments. An amount of Rs. 15,692.30 
lakhs has been provided to States for 6 Tiger Reserves till the 
completion of this Project in 2004. 
8. Other Initiatives Taken: 
— Eight more potential sites have been identified for Project Tiger 
coverage. 
— "Project Allowance" has been provided under the scheme to field staff 
working in tiger reserves. 
— Regional Monitoring of Tiger Reserves has been done by a group of 
experts as per the normative standards of the Ministry. 
— 100% Central Assistance is provided for deploying anti-poaching strike 
squads in Tiger Reserves, apart from expenditure relating to research, 
veterinary, monitoring and evaluation, compensation to the legal heir of 
staff/person killed while performing duty, and for monitoring of tiger 
population. 
— Information and communication technology is under use for linking 
important tiger reserves in the GIS Domain for evolving a 
management support system and crime detection, dissemination of 
information through web and evolving a 'National Tiger Monitoring and 
Habitat Evaluation System' with regional protocols. 
— The allocation under Project Tige r has been enhanced from Rs. 
7500 lakhs in the IX Plan to Rs. 15,000 lakhs in the X Plan.

                359.       DR.    T  .     SUBBARAMI       REDDY.                                                                                            
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the details of the rules and regulations governing prevention of food 
adulteration in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the existing laws have proved to be ineffective in 
preventing food adulteration in the country; 
(c) whether any comparative study has been undertaken between the Indian 
laws and those adopted by the Developed Nations to learn how those countries 
have succeeded in nearly eliminating food adulteration and the shortcomings 
of the Indian laws; and 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, whether such a study would be 
instituted? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) Adulteration in 
food stuffs is checked and regulated in the country under the provisions of 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rules, 1955. The Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Act has been amended thrice so far, in 1964, 1976 and 1986 to plug 
the loop-holes and make the law more stringent and also to empower the 
recognized consumer organizations to play active role in the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Programme. 
The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the rules made thereunder 
provide for adequate provisions to check and curb the adulteration and 
misbranding of food articles. The Act provides for strict penal provisions against 
the offenders. 
Standards of quality have been laid down under the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Rules, 1955 for more than 270 articles of food. Most of the rules 
and regulations laid down under these rules are in conformity with the 
guidelines laid down by the Codex Alimentarious Commission, an 
International body of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and 
World Health Organisation (WHO) of the United Nations.

WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a)to (c) WHO'S Report 
titled "Preventing Chronic Diseases -AVital Investment" has been globally 
launched recently. The report points out that 80% of chronic disease deaths occur in 
low and middle-income countries including India. The problem of chronic 
diseases (i.e. heart disease, stroke, di abetes, injuries etc.) has major adverse

at both the whole populations and individuals focusing on the common

Combating the Bird Flu 
 373.  SHRI THENNALAG BALAKRISHNA PILLAI: 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have prepared itself fully to combat the Bird Flu 
epidemic; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the decision taken in the meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) No case of Bird 
Flu (Avian Influenza) has been reported in India either in humans or birds. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry of 
Avian Influenza in to India and to cont ain the disease if it has to happen in 
poultry or humans. The measures instituted are: 
• A Joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General of Health Services constituting members from Indian 
Council of Medical Research, National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases, World Health Organizat ion and Department of Animal 
Husbandry is monitoring the situation ever since the WHO alerted the 
global community and advising appropriate actions to the 
Government. 
• The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
134 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of 
suspicion of outbreak of the disease and also in the event of 
outbreak of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A 
conference of the State Secretarie s of Animal Husbandry was held 
regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease. 
• Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal Disease 
Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. Training has been 
imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the Animal Husbandry 
Department, how to collect and dispatch the samples to the laboratory 
for testing. 
• There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. (Even 
birds [grant parent stock of poultry etc.) imported from highly pathogenic 
avian influenza free countries ar e subjected to quarantine and 
screening. 
• Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to all 
their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory birds in 
identified water bodies. Any unusual death among migratory birds would 
immediately be brought to the notice of Department of Animal 
Husbandry. 
• Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held on 1 "August,  2005 with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan. 
• A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza has 
been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal with any 
suspected outbreak. The State level action plan will be discussed with 
the State Governments, shortly. 
• The com ponents of the action plan such as hospitals strengthening, 
Influenza Surveillance Network, laboratory strengthening in terms of bio-
safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of drugs and 
Information Education Communication are being taken up in a phased 
manner. 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
• An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under the 
chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for management of Avian Influenza in the 
country. 
• National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating 
outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human Influenza 
surveillance network has been operationalised. 
• The situation has also been reviewed by Committee of Secretaries and 
Ministry of Home Affairs. 
Because of the proactive steps taken by the Government, there is no spread 
of Avian Influenza from neighbouring countries in to India.

Iodised salt and goitre 
 †376. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the methodology to prove that non-iodised salt plays a vital role in 
causing goitre and mental retardation in children in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have no means to prevent the 
diseases caused due to consumption of excess quantity of iodine by. using 
iodised salt; 
(c) if so, the rationale behind making the sale of iodised salts compulsory; and 
(d) the reasons for Government's intention for initiating an international 
debate on the issue instead of doing it at the national level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) It is well 
established medical fact that nutritional iodine deficiency results in a 
spectrum of diseases designated as Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) which 
include goitre, mental and physical retardation, still birth, neuromotor defects, 
cretins etc. Most of the Iodine deficiency disorders are permanent and incurable 
in nature except a few types of goitre, but all these can be prevented by regular 
consumption of iodised salt. 
In our country, the iodine level in salt at the consumption level is 15 ppm 
(parts per million) while at production level it is 30 ppm. The average 
consumption of iodised salt per person per day is 10 gm. Thus the 
possibility of excess consumption of iodine through iodised salt does not arise. 
The iodine level of iodised salt is absolutely safe. In Japan, the consumption 
of iodine is upto 3000 microgram per day and they have not 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
139 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
noticed any ill effects including iodine induced hyperthyroidism. Further the 
excess of iodine in the body is excreted in urine which is measured as urinary 
iodine excretion. 
About 92 countries are implementing compulsory iodisation of salt. 
Iodised salt is the most effective and cost effective way to prevent and control 
this problem. This has been well documented by WHO and UNICEF. The iodine 
deficiency disorders are prevalent in the entire country and no State/UT is free 
from goitre and other IDD. These were the reasons that led to the Governments 
took decision to ban the sale of non-iodised salt for direct human consumption 
as a public health measure.

revealed the dismal state of health status of the tribal communities in the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Ministry of Tribal Affairs had sponsored a study—Health and 
Malnutrition Study among the PTG of Sahariyas in Rajasthan—having Re-look at 
the Traditional Food Habits. The study revealed that over 80% of the Sahariyas 
are living below poverty line and have a high degree of mal nutrition and

(c) to (d) The Government has recently launched the National Rural Health 
Mission with a special emphasis on vulnerable sections of the rural population. 
The main objective of the NRHM is to provide accessible, affordable, 
accountable, effective and reliable primary health care especially to the poor and 
vulnerable sections of the population. It seeks to provide an overarching 
umbrella to the existing vertical schemes/programmes of Health and Family 
Welfare. It also aims to address the issue of health in the context of a sector wide 
approach encompassing sanitation and hygiene, nutrition safe drinking water as basic 
determinants of good health. It further seeks to build greater ownership for Health 
& Family Welfare programmes among the community through involvement of 
Panchayat Raj institutions, NGOs and othe r stakeholders at national, state, 
district and sub-district levels. 
In addition all Programme Officers have been directed to earmark 8% of their 
Annual Plan funds to the Tribal Sub-Plan for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. 
Specific Programmes like the enhanced Malaria Control Project and the Yaws 
Eradication Programme have been formulated exclusively for the tribal and 
remote areas. Keeping in view that most of the tribal population is concentrated 
in far flung areas, the population coverage norms for Primary Health Care 
infrastructure and some Disease Control Programmes have been relaxed. As 
supplementing efforts towards improving health status of tribals the Ministry of Tribal

383. SHRI C. PERUMAL Will the Mi nister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is proposed to popularize generic medicines without brand names; 
(b) if so, how the problem of spurious medicines will be tackled; 
(c) whether it is proposed to provide quality certification for medicines on 
the lines of ISI mark; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) In order to popularize 
generic medicines without brand name the Government purchases of drugs are 
generally on generic names. Also, the labeling provisions under Drugs and 
Cometics Rules had been amended to provide that the generic name of the product 
should appear in more conspicuous manner than the brand name. 
(b) Problem of spurious drug may span both branded as well as generic drug for 
which detailed guidelines have been provided to all State Drug Control 
Authorities who are the enforcing authorities to monitor quality of drugs. Strict 
penalties have been prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act for persons found 
indulging in manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. Also, the Government of 
India is providing substantial assistance to State governments under a capacity 
building project to augment drug-testing capacities of States laboratories so that 
any suspected drug can be speedily analyzed. 
(c) to (e) The standards of drugs are prescribed under the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act and rely on pharmacopoeial monographs which prescribe detailed 
quality specifications. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) does not prescribe 
quality specifications for drugs. 
The requirements of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) prescribed under 
D&C Rules are required to be adhered to by all drug-manufacturing units in the 
country. Therefore, there is no separa te certification for medicines on the line 
of ISI marks.

WHO'S report on killer diseases 
399. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Health Organization has in its recent report given a 
wake-up call to India to squarely meet the challenges of some killer diseases 
in the country. 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to meet the challenges highlighted 
in the WHO Report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMl): (a) and (b) The World 
Health Organization in its various reports in 2005 has identified the emergence 
of pandermics of SARS, Avian influenza, dengue fever, Japanese encephalitis, 
Leptosphirosis and drug resistant malaria which slowly but steadily have 
entrenched themselves in the large parts of South East Asia 
160 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Region including India. WHO has also pointed out that the recent occurrence of Avian 
influenza in various Asian countries demands greater attention by the national 
authorities to immediately strengt hen the recognitio n and response 
mechanisms, infrastructure and expertise. The WHO has also warned that these 
emerging diseases will continue to challenge public health systems for many 
years to come. A well developed strategy and programme shall have to be 
implemented through a coordinated and pragmatic plan and a vigilant public 
health system for effective containment of these diseases. 
(c) The Government has an elaborate network in place to contain diseases 
like SARS, Avian Influenza, Dengue, Japanese Encephalitis, Leprospirosis and 
drug resistant malaria. Institutions like National Institute of Communicable 
Disease (NICD) are constantly engaged in research and investigation to check 
outbreak and to control the diseases. 
The National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme (NVBDCP) is 
functional in all States to meet the challenge of Malaria, Dengue Fever and 
Japanese Encephalitis. 
To prevent spread of Avian Influenza to India, periodic reviews have been 
regularly conducted since 2003. There is an Avian Influenza Monitoring Cell in 
NICD, which has been designated the nodal agency for implementing contingency 
plan which includes forming Rapid Response Teams and stockpiling of 
Chemo prophylaxis drugs. 
For creating and sustaining strong and vigilant public health system, the 
integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) has been launched in November, 2004. 
IDSP is designed not only for surveillance and response for the diseases labeled by 
WHO as killer Diseases but also to meet the challenges of unknown diseases in future. 
A substantial part of the country has already been covered by IDSP which will 
extend to the whole country by 2006.    .

Powder) 
Indoor Residual Spraying with DDT 50% WDP had been quite effective in the 
prevention of malaria menace. IRS with DDT remains effective for a period of 2 to

the period of malaria transmission season. However, in the areas where the malaria 
vectors have developed resistance to DDT, it has been replaced with other group 
of insecticides.

Indoor Residual Spraying with Malathion 25% WDP had been quite 
effective in the prevention of malari a menace. IRS with Malathion remains 
effective for a period of 1 to 2 months and hence 3 rounds of IRS are carried 
in different States depending upon the pe riod of malaria transmission season. 
However, in the areas where the malaria vectors have developed resistance to 
Malathion, it is replaced with other group of insecticides. 
3. Synthetic Pyrethroid Group: This is a new group of insecticides. 
There are many compounds in this group of insecticides. However, the 
following insecticides of this group are being used in malaria control

carried to cover States depending upon the period of malaria transmission season. In areas

(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Justice G. C. Garg Commission in his report

on account of a gap created in the continuity of the long welded right rail of the 
up track on 26.11.1998. Rear right trolley of coach No. 10 of the Up train derailed

derailed/capsized coaches of the Up trai n. The cause as established by the 
Commission has been accepted by the Government. 
Directorate of Track Procurement of Railway Board, Northern Railway, 
Director General of Supplies & Disposal and Bhilai Steel Plant of Steel 
Authority of India Limited have been  held equally responsible. Primary 
responsibility of engine crew of Up train has also been accepted.

Western Railway and Diesel Loco Modernisation Works, were accused of sexual

*65. SHRI VIJAYJ. DARDA:† 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Amended Cable TV Network Rules, 1994 make foreign 
channel operators (Discovery, Ten Sports, Star Network and HBO) more 
accountable, as now they will have to register themselves by depositing 
Rs. 1.5 crore and also nominating an Indian for telecasting their 
programmes in the country; 
(b) if so, whether a special mechanism has been evolved for this purpose; and 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Vijay J. Darda. 
12 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, whether the discrepancies, if any, detected in their programmes 
would be taken care of? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
PRIYA RANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Government has recently issued Policy Guidelines for 
Downlinking of Television Channels, which provide that no person/entity 
shall downlink a channel that has not been registered with the Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting under these guidelines. It further provides 
all persons/entities desirous of downlinking TV channels shall be required 
to obtain permission from Ministry of  Information and Broadcasting in 
accordance with the terms and conditions prescribed under these 
guidelines. As a result of these guidelines, the local delivery service 
providers i.e. cable operator and DT H service providers will distribute 
only registered TV channels. 
The eligibility criteria prescribed in  the guidelines for the applicant 
company seeking permission to downlink TV channel, inter-alia include: 
• Possessing a net worth of Rs. 1.5 crores and Rs. 1 crore for 
every additional channel. 
• It must be a company registered in India under the Indian Companies 
Act, 1956, irrespective of equity structure, foreign ownership or 
management control. 
• The applicant company must have a commercial presence in India 
with its principal place of business in India. 
• The applicant company to provide details of their Directors and key 
executives to obtain their national security clearance. 
Every company permitted to downlink channels uplinked from other 
countries shall have to pay Rs. 5 lakhs as the initial fee. Similarly for 
each channel to be registered a fee of Rs. 5.00 lakhs for initial registration 
for five years will have to be paid. In addition an annual fee for Rs. 1.00 
lakh per channel is payable. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2005] 
The applicant person/entity desirous to downlink channels will be issued 
permission and certificate of registration after completion of the 
procedures laid down in the downlinking guidelines. 
TV channels transmitted/retransmitted through the Cable TV Network 
and DTH Network are required to adhere to the Programme and 
Advertising Code prescribed in the Cable TV Network Rules, 1994, in 
accordance with the Cable TV Network (Regulation) Act, 1995 and DTH 
guidelines respectively. An Inter-ministerial Committee is already looking 
into violation of the Codes and action is being taken against the channels 
violating the codes from time to time. 
Now through the downlinking guidelines, adherence to these codes 
has also been made obligatory upon all channels uplinking from abroad 
and downlinked into India and violations of conditions of downlinking will 
invite further action.

Puppet shows 
*63. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of CULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government had held any puppet shows for the children 
on the occasion of the International Puppetry Day recently; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the amount incurred; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government to increase the awareness 
about the puppet shows among kids? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. On the occasion of International Puppetry Day, a festival and 
exhibition 'PutuI Yatra' was organised on Indian puppets in Mumbai. The 
Festival had as many as ten performances of puppeteers from all over 
India. A workshop on 'Role of Puppetry in Education' was also organised 
during this occasion at Guwahati. 
(c) An amount of Rs. 23.62 lakhs was incurred on these programmes. 
(d) Workshops and training programmes have been conducted by 
Sangeet Natak Akademi in the field of puppetry providing a platform for 
children to learn manipulation techniques, making of puppets, singing of 
folk songs etc. Awards to pupp eteers, grants to institutions, 
documentation, exhibitions and fest ivals of puppetry are included in 
Akademi's regular support to puppetry. Akademi also holds monthly shows 
of puppetry and interaction in Delhi and has screened films to increase 
awareness about the art. 
The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) has been 
offering Puppetry as a teaching tool in order to disseminate information 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2005] 
on Indian culture to children.. Their regular programme includes 
scholarships to children and awards to school teachers for popularizing 
puppetry. They organize workshops on Role of Puppetry in Education in 
which a number of local students participate. 
The Ministry of Culture has been offering scholarships for all types of 
puppet theatre. Production grants, buildings grants and salary grants have 
also been given to institutions involved in puppetry. 
Abolition of quota and reservation in private institutions 
*67. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court of India has recently ruled that 
Government's requirement that the private institutions which do not receive 
any State aid, should also follow Government's policy on reservation of 
seats for the backward classes, is a serious encroachment on the rights 
and autonomy of these institutions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) Government's reaction thereto and the steps, if any, proposed in 
this regard; 
 
(d) Whether Government have constituted any committee for 
monitoring the fee-structure in the private institutes; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The Supreme Court observed in the case of 
PA. Inamdar and ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra and ors. that the State 
cannot impose its reservation policy on minority and non-minority unaided 
private institutions. According to the order of the Supreme Court neither 
the policy of reservation can be enforced by the State nor any quota or 
percentage of admissions can be carved out to be appropriated by the 
State in a minority or non-minority  unaided private institution. The 
Government is in the process of evolving a common national approach 
to this important issue which addresses national, social and constitutional 
imperatives in a holistic manner. 
28 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) and (e) The Supreme Court in its judgment in the case of Islamic 
Academy of Education and others Vs. State of Karnataka and others 
have directed the State Governments to constitute a Fee Committee to 
determine the fee structure in unaided institutions in respective States.

Punishment to rapists 
*70. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
SHRI VIJAYJ. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that law provides punishment for the proven 
guilt of rape "a minimum of 7 years imprisonment" still many courts have 
30 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
either awarded lesser years of imprisonment and High Courts have even 
reduced the sentences in such cases; and 
(b) if so, whether Government would ensure that maximum 
punishment, as provided in the law, be awarded in proven cases to deter 
the prospective perpetrators of this heinous crime? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H. R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) Section 376 of Indian Penal Code (IPC) prescribes a punishment of a 
minimum period of seven years of imprisonment and a maximum 
punishment of life imprisonment for the offence of rape. However, in a 
few serious cases of rapes like rape of a girl below 12 years of age and 
custodial rape, the minimum punishment could be 10 years. As per proviso 
to the above Section, the court may, for adequate and special reasons to 
be mentioned in the judgement, impose a sentence of imprisonment for 
a term less than seven years. 
(b) As the judiciary is independent, it is not possible for the Government 
to interfere in the functioning of the judiciary.

Regulation Act, 1995 prescribes that all television channels transmitted/ 
retransmitted through the cable network are required to adhere to the 
programme and advertisement code prescribed thereunder. These codes 
prohibit telecast of any obscene or vulgar programme/advertisement. 
The Government has taken the following steps to ensure adherence to 
these codes:— 
(i) The Central Government has constituted an inter ministerial 
committee to look into violations of the codes. On 
recommendation of the Committee action is taken against 
channels for violating the codes. This is an on going process. 
(ii) Action for violation of codes can also be taken by any authorized 
officer i.e. DM, SDM or Commissioner of Police or any other 
officer notified in the official gazette by the Central Government 
or State Government under the Cable Act.

Professionalisation of Management 
*78. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of heavy industrial undertakings and public enterprises 
where professionalisation of top management has been introduced as a 
policy initiative, and whether the same would percolate down in the 
hierarchy; 
(b) whether there has been any marked gain or improvement in 
performance as a result of this process and how long it would take to 
complete this process in all units of this sector; 
(c) the number of the units already closed, those in operation and 
economic viability of the running units; and 
(d) the future prospects of these units, category-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN 
DEV): (a) As far as the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) under 
the Department of Heavy Industry are concerned, vacancies are being 
filled as per the policy guidelines for full time and as well as for Independent 
Directors. Policy below the Board level posts is framed by the respective 
PSEs themselves depending upon their professional requirements. 
(b) Filling up of the Board level po sts is a contin uous process and 
actions in anticipation of a vacancy are initiated well in advance to ensure 
timely filling up of such posts. Improvement in performance of a PSE is 
dependent upon a wide range of factors including technology, processes, 
market conditions, status of econ omy, competitivenes s etc. besides 
contribution of the top management on policy initiatives. 
(c) and (d) Out of 48 PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry, 
11 have been closed and 3 are not in operation. There are 9 profit making 
PSEs and the remaining 25 are incurring loss. Efforts for revival of sick/ 
loss making PSEs through the Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector 
Enterprises (BRPSE) are continuing for improving the viability of the 
enterprises. In the case of 5 PSEs, revival plans have been aproved by 
Government with expectations of sustained viability as projected in their 
revival plans.

Ban on contesting elections 
† 548. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that all political parties have recently held 
discussions for evolving consensus on the suggestion given by the election 
commission that persons having more than 2 children should not be allowed 
to contest election; and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b)The Constitution (Seventy-ninth 
Amendment) Bill, 1992 was introduced in Rajya Sabha in December, 1992. 
Under the provisions of the Bill a person shall be disqualified for being 
chosen as, and for being a member of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly or, as the case may be, either of the Legislature of the State, 
if he/she has more than two children. However, it will not apply to those who 
already have more than two children or those who beget an additional child 
within one year of the commencement of the Act. The Bill was referred to the 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development for 
examination. The Committee examined the Bill and recommended the Bill for 
passage without any change. 
While recommending the Bill for passage, the Committee also 
recommended that the Government may convene a meeting of leaders of 
various political parties in Parliament to ensure the passage of the Bill. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
150 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Accordingly, meetings were held on 14th August, 1997- and 13th 
December, 1999. However, no consensus could emerge in these 
meetings. In the last meeting held on 13th December, 1999, many leaders were 
of the view that the Bill needs to be withdrawn from the Rajya Sabha. This issue 
was discussed in the meeting of the Consultative Committee of the Parliament 
on 2nd May, 2003, where a consensus emerged among the Members on the 
need for more effective measures for controlling population growth in the 
country. It was felt that there was need for larger consensus on the matter, for 
which a meeting of leaders of political parties could be convened. However, 
since the policy of the Government is to keep the family welfare programme 
as voluntary and free from any incentives, disincentives or coercion, the option 
of withdrawing the Bill is under consideration of the Government.

THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH):(a) and 
(c) The tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes in 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2005] 
respect of forest land, which they have been traditionally in-habiting for 
ages have not been adequately recognized under the existing rules and 
guidelines. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs was mandated to formulate a 
comprehensive Central Legislation to redress this historical injustice done 
to the forest dwelling tribal communities and for clear assertion of their 
legal rights on land and other traditional rights. 
This Ministry accordingly prepared a draft "Scheduled Tribes 
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005" to provide a legislative frame 
for recognition of forest rights of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries and other stakeholders. The 
draft Bill proposed to recognize such rights on land, minor forest produce, 
etc. of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes. The Bill was posted on the website 
of the Ministry seeking comments of the public and all stakeholders till-
10.7.2005. The Ministry has received comments/suggestions from a large 
number of individuals/organizations, either supporting the Bill or opposing 
the same on various grounds. In the light of comments/suggestions 
received, the draft Bill has been further modified to reconcile the twin 
objective of undoing historical injustice done to the tribal communities 
with the concern for environmental protection. The proposed Bill is, 
however, still a tentative draft Bill and to be finalized as per the established 
procedure. No time frame can be i ndicated for its introduction in the 
Parliament.

Concern over the extent of poverty in the country 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): Sir, thank you for giving me an 
opportunity to raise my Special Mention. My Special Mention is regarding 
confusion relating to the extent of poverty in India. There is a 40 per cent 
divergence between the poverty estimates of the National Accounts 
Statistics (NAS) and those of the National Survey Organization (NSSO). 
The Planning Commission's poverty estimate of 26 per cent is based on 
the 55th round conducted by NSSO in 1999-2000. If one were to believe 
in the NAS, our poverty levels are down to 15 per cent. Moreover, the 
55th NSS round changed its methodology, giving rise to problems of 
comparability with the earlier rounds. The 50th round of NSS in 1993-94 
estimated poverty of 37 per cent, based on a 30-day recall period for all 
items of consumption. Alongside this 30-day recall method, a separate 
questionnaire was used which deployed different recall periods, 9-day, 
30-day and 365-day. Such anomalies should be addressed and the 
change explained in a transparent manner so that data is neither open to 
political misuse nor it given a distorted view relating to prevalence of the 
extent of poverty in India. Unless a fairly exact extent of poverty is known, 
its effective tackling becomes impracticable leading to wastage of financial 
resources deployed towards mitigat ing poverty, and, simultaneously, 
poverty removal programmes, being launched by the Government, from 
time to time, missing pre-determined targets. In 2000, the World Bank 
did observe that Indian reforms deepened inequality which obviously does 
not square with our high growth rate. The Planning Commission, NSSO 
and NAS must initiate measures immediately to enforce built-in 
safeguards so as to avoid vast difference in arriving poverty figures by 
the surveying authorities.

Concern over suicide by farmers in Vidarbha, Maharashtra 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, through this Special Mention, I wish to draw the attention 
of the House and of the Government of  India to the tragic situation of 
farmers of Vidarbha region of Maharashtra where during the last three 
weeks, over 105 farmers have committed suicide. 
All the districts of Vidarbha are victims of excessive flooding and rainfall 
earlier this year. In many parts, cotton crop, the mainstay of farmers, was 
badly damaged. The cotton of Vidarbha region is subject to the tyranny 
of the Maharashtra Cotton Monopoly Procurement Scheme. Under the 
scheme, the farmers are paid a guaranteed price on delivery of cotton. 
This guaranteed price, according to a decision made by the present 
Minister of Agriculture, who was then the Chief Minister of Maharashtra, 
has to be 20 per cent above the minimum support price for cotton. This 
premium was supposed to be a compensation to the farmers for the 
deprivation of the freedom of access to market. Last year, the Government 
of Maharashtra offered the farmers a price of Rs.2,300 per quintal. 
However, a part of that payment was not made till the Diwali festivities. 
That is one reason why there was a spate of suicides on the eve of the 
festival. 
186 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
Recently, Dr. M.S. Swaminathan, Chairman of the National Farm 
Commission, who was on a visit to the Vidarbha region, stated 
unequivocally that the credit structure was responsible for the high number 
of suicides in the region. It is reported that he also went on to mention 
that the Government of Maharashtra should pay the farmers, irrespective 
of all considerations, a price of Rs.3000 per tonne. 
Unfortunately, the Government of Maharashtra is insisting on paying nothing 
more than the minimum support price as a guaranteed price this year. 
Sir, I urge upon the Government of India to intervene in the matter and 
order the Government of Maharashtra to pay the cotton farmers a 
Guaranteed price of Rs.2,000 and a final price of Rs.3,000 per tonne as 
recommended by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan; otherwise initiate a damage 
control action immediately so that no cotton producing farmer from 
Maharashtra is driven to suicide hereafter. Thank you.

Concern over depletion of ground water levels in various parts of                    
                                                the country 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, there is a serious 
concern in many parts of the count ry among policy-makers as well as 
farmers about the depletion of ground water as well as salinity in ground 
water. In the Deccan plateau States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and 
Maharashtra, the ground water levels have reached an alarmingly low 
level of 600 ft. and above. So much so, in many villages, in the summer 
months of 2005, the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, 
Maharashtra and others have to supply drinking water by tankers. The 
farmers are digging borewells indisc riminately. Instead of consulting 
experts, they are depending on locals to identify the digging points. This 
is causing huge losses to the farmers, as the failure rate of digging wells 
is as high as 80 per cent. Moreover, individual farmers do not maintain 
the distance between each borewell. 
Similarly, in the States of West Bengal, Orissa, Assam, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, farmers are using diesel motors, which are proving 
to be very expensive to the farmers. In many cases, 25-30 per cent of the 
cost of production is spent on diesel. Individual farmers do not take water 
conservation practices into consideration even in the Rabi season even 
though availability of water as well as electricity is limited. 
I would, in this context, suggest that the task of optimising ground 
water and also controlling digging of borwells, adopting suitable cropping 
188 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
pattern should be entrusted to the local Panchayats. Farmers' committees 
should be empowered to supervise digging of wells, decide cropping 
pattern and decide in equity in water utilisation.

DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY (Karnataka): Sir, Dioxin is a super-toxic 
chemical which is formed as a by-product of the manufacture, moulding 
or burning of organic chemicals and plastics that contain chlorine. It is 
the nastiest and most toxic man-made organic chemical. Its toxicity is 
second only to radioactive waste. The House can well imagine the hazards 
this toxic chemical can pose to human health. Now it has been reported 
that eggs in our country contain dioxins. It is highly likely that this harmful 
chemical may be present in other animal products. I, therefore, request 
the Central Government that a proper study may be conducted to find 
out the level of dioxins present in eggs, meat and milk and milk products.

Concern over old railway bridges and culverts in the country 
SHRIMATI VANGAGEETHA(Andhra Pradesh): Sir, there is an urgent 
need to draw the Government's attention to railway bridges and culverts 
that were constructed 100 years ago in the South Central Railways and 
across the country. For instance, about 800 bridges and culverts in the 
South Central Railway are more than 100 years old and have outlived 
their utility a long time ago. There are 13,170 railway bridges and culverts 
in the South Central Railway Zone. Mo st of these British-built bridges 
and culverts have crossed their esti mated life-span of hundred years. 
Another about 700 structures have co mpleted 80 years of existence. 
Although a number of culverts exist like endangered species, they have 
not attracted the eyes of the Railways. The Valigonda Railway Bridge in 
Andhra Pradesh, on which the ill-fated Delta Fast Passenger train plunged

number of trains, including the super fast trains pass everyday carrying 
lakhs of passengers, in the light of the fate of Valigonda culverts. Hence 
I request the Ministry of Railways to take necessary steps immediately 
and evolve a programme for replacing these bridges without any delay.

Demand to restrict import of Arecanut and announce minimum 
support price to protect Arecanut growers of Karnataka and 
other parts of the country 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karna taka) Sir, arecanut is an 
important horticulture crop of our country. No one can think of chewing a 
paan without arecanut and paan is liked and consumed throughout the 
country. Arecanut is also consumed as meethi supari and it is an integral 
part of paan masala, etc. There are red as we ll as white varieties of 
arecanut. It is mainly grown in my  home State, Karnataka, Kerala and 
Assam. Karnataka is the largest producing State of arecanut, area, 
quantity and quality-wise and is grown in over two lakh of hectares of 
land and thousands of families are dependent on this crop for their 
livelihood. 
The prices of arecanut in Karnataka and elsewhere have crashed 
because large quantities of arecanut is being imported from Bangladesh, 
Burma, Indonesia, Thailand and Sri Lanka. The import has increased 
phenomenally and this sort of quantitative dumping has devastated the 
domestic market of arecanut. Moreover, the imported arecanut is of very 
poor quality and at the time of importing, there is no quality inspection in 
places like ports and airports. The poor quality is affecting the health of 
consumers. 
The crash in prices of arecanut has put the growers into distress 
condition. The State Government of Karnataka is trying its best to intervene 
in the market to stabilize the prices but in vain because arecanut is out of 
MSP regime. I, therefore, demand from the Central Government to, 
(a) impose reasonable restrictions on the import of arecanut to save 
the arecanut growers of Karnataka and other parts of the country;

neighbouring countries to protect the health of the consumers;

These steps should be taken on priority.

Demand for central legislation to restore reservations in private 
professional colleges in the country 
SHRI PENUMALLIMADHU (Andhra Pradesh): The Supreme Court's 
judgement of August 12, 2005 setting aside the reservation for the 
meritorious and the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students in 
the private professional  colleges is beset with serious consequences. 
Henceforth, Dalits, Girijans, Backward Classes and other poorer and 
weaker sections of the society w ould not have entry into the private 
professional colleges as hitherto. Because of the special historical factors, 
provisions were made in the Constitution of India for reservation to enable 
the traditionally oppressed classes to catch up with the rest of the society. 
This judgement is a blow to this core concept and provides an impetus to 
commercialisation of higher educ ation where only profit dominates. 
Professional education would hencefo rth be the exclusive privilege of 
the rich.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir. It is with great plea sure that I get up to speak on an 
important Bill, but have even greater pleasure to follow Mr. S.S. Ahluwalia, 
the hon. Member, with whom one gets a very rare opportunity to agree. 
Mr. Ahluwalia has, in a very uncharacteristic statesmanlike and 
constructive speech, laid out his support for the Bill. And I, in fact, support 
most of what he says, exc ept that little bit of pat ernity that he tried to 
claim for his party. I do want to remind him that this idea has been 
germinating on the public agenda over the past decade or so. In the last 
15 years, India has had six major earthquakes; it has had four major 
cyclones; it has had Tsunami; it has had innumerable floods. But for one 
reason or the other, the idea of creating a National Disaster Management 
Authority has eluded the administration, whatever the nature of the political 
party in power may be. And I want to congratulate the Home Minister for 
having finally belled the cat, taken a step forward, brought forward this 
legislation and created the National Disaster Management Authority. Now, 
I think, the main objective is to look ahead. 
Sir, I want to make four major points in my intervention. I want to make 
a few remarks on the Bill itself, even though the hon. Minister has come 
forward with some amendments. Secondly, I want to talk about some

financing issues as far as disaster management is concerned. Thirdly, I 
want to talk about the limitations of this Bill, particularly in view of the 
experience that the Gujarat State Government has had because as we 
know/Gujarat is the only State Government which has an Act, the Disaster 
Management Act, and it has a Gujarat State Disaster Management 
Authority as well. And the fourth point I want to make is on science and 
technology. I agree with Mr. Ahluwalia that we have much to learn from 
traditional knowledge, from Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita and all that. 
But I think we would be making a grave mistake if we don't realise that 
we need to make major investments in modern science and technology 
in order to meet disasters and I do want to make some points on this 
issue. Then, I will make a few concluding remarks. 
Sir, on the Bill itself, I would like to make a few comments for the hon. 
Minister's consideration. I want to begin by saying that he has already 
mentioned that a non-statutory National Disaster Management Authority 
has been, in fact, set up under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister; 
and I do want to underscore two issues, as far as the non-statutory part 
of the NDMA is concerned, it will get statutory basis at the end of tomorrow 
when the Lok Sabha also passes this Bill and after the President's 
assent. I believe that it is very  important. The NDMA, as currently 
structured, does not have a scientist or a technologist as a member. I 
know in the original notification, notifying the NDMA, there was, in fact, a 
technologist. But to the best of my knowledge - I have checked as of 
yesterday — there is no scientist or there is no technologist who is a 
member of the NDMA. And I do believe that this is a very grave omission 
and I hope this lacuna will be filled. Secondly, I think, taking up from what 
Mr. Ahluwalia was saying, the NDMA is in need of representation from 
the civil society, ultimately, disaster management, relief, rehabilitation 
and reconstruction involves partnerships betw een Governments and 
civil society, and it is very important to have at the highest policy-
making authority, at the national level, at the State level and also at the 
district level, since we are having a three-tier structure, representatives 
of a civil society, and I will explain by giving some examples why this is 
of particular importance. Sir, as far as i am concerned, the formation 
of the National Disaster Response Force in chapter VIII of the Bill is a 
very major step forward in disaster management. The Home Minister 
has already said that eight battalions , drawn from various para-military 
outfits, are going to form the

core of the National Disaster Response Force, and I would imagine that 
this would not be a top-down Disaster Management Force. This would 
have field formations, this would be located in strategic parts across the 
country. We have areas like the North-East, where the logistics are very,

approach towards disaster management that is going to bring relief and 
rehabilitation very quickly. Therefore, I think, while we set up a 
decentralised force, we need to look at it in its larger context of deployment 
in different parts of the country. 
I think, Sir, the second point that I want to make on the Bill is that while 
we have a National Disaster Management Authority, we have a State-
level Disaster Management Authority and we have a District-level Disaster

approach. The real focus is to equip the District Disaster Management

legislation—I know all of this cannot be put in the legislation—it is the 
working of the legislation that is going to be important. The focus should 
not be so much on the NDMA or the SDMA; the focus really should be 
on the District Disaster Management Authorities, and the empowerment 
of the District Disaster Management Authorities, the financial 
empowerment, the technological empowerment, and their administrative 
empowerment, that is going to be crucial, and indeed, this is the one 
lesson that we learnt from tsunami, this is the one lesson that we learnt 
from earthquake relief, this is the one lesson that we learnt from flood

disaster-fighting capability at the local level, which in our context, really 
means the district level. So, while I welcome this whole systematic 
approach to disaster management, from the national level to the State

I come to clause 1. The clause 1 says that different dates may be 
appointed for different provisions of th is Act in different States. In my 
opinion, it would not be proper. The reason I tell you. I will give two glaring 
examples from the past experience in these kinds of legislations. In 1962, 
the Advocates Act came, where section 35 is yet to be notified despite 
the repeated directions from the Supreme Court. Then recently we had 
repealed the Monopolies Restricted Practices Act. We had also brought 
in the Competition Act, in which there was a clause saying that different 
provisions will be notified on different dates. The Act is yet to be notified 
fully, there is a lot of confusion. And, the Supreme Court has come down 
heavily. The Tribunal, created under the repealed Act, is continuing. This 
is the result of bringing these kinds of clauses. This is a disastrous clause. 
I appeal to the hon. Minister either he should bring in the Act and make it 
applicable all over the country or he should keep it in abeyance till he 
feels it right to bring if forward. The reason behind this is that whenever

there is a calamity or a disaster at  a particular place, this Act would 
definitely be implemented. It means, this Act would implemented. It means, 
this Act would be applied only when a disastrous situation arises. And, 
under other circumstances, there is  no point in applying the clauses, 
stage-by-stage, in a piecemeal manner. So, I would like to request you to 
kindly reconsider clause I, and whenever it is implemented, it should be 
implemented all over the country. 
Now, I come to definition of 'disaster' I appreciate the Home Ministry, 
and the Home Minister, in particular, for the human touch involved in this. 
The definition of 'disaster' as per my reading, will not include only the 
natural calamities, like, tsunami or earthquake or flood, but it will also 
include railway accidents because the definition says," ..by accident." It 
means it will also include the railway accidents and the aeroplane 
accidents. So, this Act would be applicable to such disasters also. If 
someone wants to apply this Act, don't restrict it. Apply it fully because 
this Act is brought in with a human touch. It has be made applicable in 
the case of the railway accidents and the bus to accidents also. Then, it 
will also be applicable in the case of human negligence also. Whenever 
there is disastrous situation because of the human negligence, this Act 
will apply. Because of negligence on the part of one railway employee, a 
train may get derailed. So, there also this Act will apply. This Act will not 
apply in natural calamities only. In addition to that, it will apply to crop 
failures also because the latter portion of the clause says, "destruction of 
property due to environmental factors . " There is the failure of Bt. Cotton 
in Maharashtra. So, I appeal to the hon. Minister to have more broad-
based applicability of this Act and to have a large-hearted approach while 
applying this Act. This is my personal request. Let your bureaucrats not 
resist it later because your definit ion paves the way for a well-spread 
applicability, and the horizon of applicability is much more than what we 
could visualise. This is what definition could indicate, sir. 
Then, I could say, there is one sm all problem in drafting Clause of 
3(2). Clause 3(2) says this way, "The National Authority shall consist of 
such number of Members not exceeding ten, as may be prescribed by 
the Central Government and unless the rules otherwise provide,..." That 
means the ten can be increased if the rules indicate. Suppose, a rule is 
framed for extending more number of persons, then, it can be enlarged, 
it means that. Sir, I appeal to you that no rule could override an enactment.

what will happen, Sir? So, despite the discretion given to the persons, 
however high he may be, whatever highests office he could have, regional

there is a calamity is a calamity in particular State, and you want to give

add in that, at least, for a temporary time. You must have the Act in such

among the ten, the affected State should be represented automatically 
so that the person could meet t he Prime Minister and tell what the 
requirement is. Don't confine to ten, have a large heart to include the 
affected State representation also, if it is hot represented among the ten. 
This is my humble submission, sir. 
Then, Sir, I feel yet another problem in drafting clause 7. Sir, kindly 
see Clause 7. It says, "The National Authority may constitute an Advisory 
Committee to look after the matter at the national level." Sir, who is 
appointing? The National Authority can appoint an advisory Committee 
at the National level. There is logic. Kindly read the next sentence, 
"...Management at the National, State and District level..." Kindly see 
clause17. Let us have a comparat ive study. When clause 17 clearly 
illustrates that the state authority shall have its own advisory Committee 
and they will appoint district Advisory Committee, where is the need 
under Clause 7 for the Central Advisory Committee to appoint a State 
level Advisory Committee and the District level Advisory Committee? So, 
both are clashing with each other. So, please confine yourself under 
Clause 7.
